Example: access to schools and health care in Recife and Caruaru

Source: vignettes/articles/recife-caruaru.Rmd
recife-caruaru.Rmd

The other examples on this site use small sample networks. This one starts from nothing, as a study of a real city would: it downloads the streets of two cities of Pernambuco, Brazil, from OpenStreetMap, places their residents on a grid with the census, takes the public schools and the primary health care units from the official registers, and measures how long it takes to reach the nearest of each, walking, cycling and driving.

  • Recife, the state capital (1.49 million people in the Censo 2022), on the coast, flat, crossed by rivers. Its street network is cut with 10 km around the municipality, which takes in the core of the metropolitan area (Olinda, Jaboatão dos Guararapes, Camaragibe and parts of Paulista and São Lourenço da Mata), so trips near the border can end in a neighbouring municipality.
  • Caruaru, 130 km inland in the Agreste (378 thousand people), a compact city in a large, mostly rural municipality, with 5 km around it.

Everything below is one script, and every step works for any Brazilian municipality: change the IBGE code and the buffer. The output shown is what it prints; it was computed on 2026-11-11.

Streets only. No public, openly licensed GTFS feed was found for the buses of the Grande Recife Consórcio de Transporte or the metro (CBTU): it is not on the open-data portals of the city, the state or CBTU, nor in the Mobility Database. Caruaru has none either. So this example routes on the streets, and leaves public transport out rather than approximate it. With a GTFS feed, the same code takes mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT") and a departure time: the Recife metropolitan region example does that, with the feed the consortium publishes on its own site (found after this page was written; it states no licence).

The data

Data Source Licence
Streets OpenStreetMap, extract of the Nordeste region by Geofabrik, dated 2026-11-01 (445 MB) ODbL 1.0
Municipal boundaries IBGE, malhas municipais (API, version 3) public data, IBGE
Population IBGE, Censo Demográfico 2022, census tracts with their population, variable v0001 (44 MB for Pernambuco) public data, IBGE
Schools INEP, Catálogo de Escolas 2023, with the coordinates of each school, as published by Ipea’s geobr (schools_2023, 101 MB for Brazil) public data, INEP; geobr is MIT
Health units CNES, Ministério da Saúde, through OpenDataSUS (cnes_estabelecimentos_csv.zip, 57 MB for Brazil, updated daily; downloaded on 2026-11-11) open data, Ministério da Saúde

The files are downloaded once into a directory of their own (set PEABIRU_EXAMPLE_DATA to keep it somewhere else). Cutting the extract needs osmium (brew install osmium-tool, apt install osmium-tool, or conda-forge).

library(peabiru)
library(sf)

data_dir <- Sys.getenv("PEABIRU_EXAMPLE_DATA", "pe-data")
raw <- file.path(data_dir, "raw")
dir.create(raw, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
options(timeout = 3600)   # the extract is 445 MB

fetch <- function(url, name = basename(url)) {
  dest <- file.path(raw, name)
  if (!file.exists(dest)) download.file(url, dest, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  dest
}
nordeste <- fetch("https://download.geofabrik.de/south-america/brazil/nordeste-261101.osm.pbf")
tracts_file <- fetch(paste0("https://ftp.ibge.gov.br/Censos/Censo_Demografico_2022/",
                            "Agregados_por_Setores_Censitarios/malha_com_atributos/",
                            "setores/gpkg/UF/PE/PE_setores_CD2022.gpkg"))
schools_file <- fetch("https://www.ipea.gov.br/geobr/data_gpkg/schools/2023/schools_2023.gpkg")
cnes_file <- fetch(paste0("https://s3.sa-east-1.amazonaws.com/ckan.saude.gov.br/CNES/",
                          "cnes_estabelecimentos_csv.zip"))

cities <- data.frame(key = c("recife", "caruaru"),
                     code = c("2611606", "2604106"),   # IBGE codes
                     buffer = c(10000, 5000))          # metres
utm <- 31985   # SIRGAS 2000 / UTM zone 25S, in metres, for both cities

Streets: the municipality and a buffer

The boundary of each municipality comes from IBGE’s API. Buffered in metres, it is the polygon osmium extract cuts the regional extract with; the cut goes in a directory of its own, which build_network() reads.

boundary_of <- function(code) {
  url <- paste0("https://servicodados.ibge.gov.br/api/v3/malhas/municipios/", code,
                "?formato=application/vnd.geo+json&qualidade=maxima")
  b <- st_read(fetch(url, paste0(code, ".geojson")), quiet = TRUE)
  st_transform(st_make_valid(b), utm)
}

cut_streets <- function(key, boundary, buffer) {
  dir <- file.path(data_dir, key, "network")
  dir.create(dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  polygon <- file.path(data_dir, key, "cut.geojson")
  st_write(st_transform(st_buffer(boundary, buffer), 4326), polygon,
           delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
  pbf <- file.path(dir, paste0(key, ".osm.pbf"))
  status <- system2("osmium", c("extract", "--overwrite", "-p", polygon, nordeste, "-o", pbf))
  stopifnot(status == 0)
  dir
}

boundaries <- lapply(setNames(cities$code, cities$key), boundary_of)
networks <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(cities))) {
  k <- cities$key[i]
  dir <- cut_streets(k, boundaries[[k]], cities$buffer[i])
  networks[[k]] <- build_network(dir)
  cat(sprintf("%-8s %5.1f MB\n", k, file.size(file.path(dir, paste0(k, ".osm.pbf"))) / 1e6))
}
#> recife    16.0 MB
#> caruaru    1.9 MB
networks$recife
#> <peabiru_network>
#>   data path: pe-data/recife/network
#>   streets:   104,331 vertices, 275,968 edges
#>   transit:   none (no GTFS feed)
#>   elevation: NONE
networks$caruaru
#> <peabiru_network>
#>   data path: pe-data/caruaru/network
#>   streets:   28,445 vertices, 78,318 edges
#>   transit:   none (no GTFS feed)
#>   elevation: NONE

Where people live: a hexagonal grid with the census

The census counts people by tract, and tracts vary from a city block to hundreds of square kilometres. A regular grid makes the cities comparable: hexagons 500 m apart, numbered row by row from the south-west, over the whole municipality. Each cell gets the population of the tracts it covers, in proportion to the area it covers of each.

hex_grid <- function(area, spacing = 500) {
  b <- st_bbox(area)
  h <- spacing * sqrt(3) / 2
  centres <- expand.grid(i = -1:(ceiling((b[["xmax"]] - b[["xmin"]]) / spacing) + 1),
                         j = -1:(ceiling((b[["ymax"]] - b[["ymin"]]) / h) + 1))
  centres$x <- b[["xmin"]] + centres$i * spacing + (centres$j %% 2) * spacing / 2
  centres$y <- b[["ymin"]] + centres$j * h
  k <- (30 + 60 * 0:6) * pi / 180   # pointy side up
  r <- spacing / sqrt(3)
  cells <- st_sfc(lapply(seq_len(nrow(centres)), function(n)
    st_polygon(list(cbind(centres$x[n] + r * cos(k), centres$y[n] + r * sin(k))))),
    crs = st_crs(area))
  cells <- cells[lengths(st_intersects(cells, area)) > 0]
  st_sf(id = seq_along(cells), geometry = cells)
}

population_grid <- function(code, boundary) {
  tracts <- st_read(tracts_file, quiet = TRUE, query = paste0(
    "SELECT v0001, geom FROM PE_setores_CD2022 WHERE CD_MUN = '", code, "'"))
  tracts <- st_transform(st_make_valid(tracts), utm)
  tracts$tract_area <- as.numeric(st_area(tracts))
  cells <- hex_grid(boundary)
  parts <- suppressWarnings(st_intersection(cells, tracts))
  parts$people <- parts$v0001 * as.numeric(st_area(parts)) / parts$tract_area
  people <- tapply(parts$people, parts$id, sum)
  cells$population <- 0
  cells$population[match(as.integer(names(people)), cells$id)] <- people
  centres <- st_coordinates(st_transform(st_centroid(st_geometry(cells)), 4326))
  cells$lon <- round(centres[, 1], 6)
  cells$lat <- round(centres[, 2], 6)
  cells$id <- as.character(cells$id)
  cells[cells$population > 0, ]
}

grids <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(cities))) {
  k <- cities$key[i]
  grids[[k]] <- population_grid(cities$code[i], boundaries[[k]])
  cat(sprintf("%-8s %5d cells, %s people\n", k, nrow(grids[[k]]),
              format(round(sum(grids[[k]]$population)), big.mark = ",")))
}
#> recife    1107 cells, 1,488,797 people
#> caruaru   4489 cells, 378,048 people

The Censo 2022 counts 1,488,924 people in Recife and 378,048 in Caruaru; the grid keeps all but 127 in Recife, in tracts that reach slightly outside IBGE’s municipal boundary. Caruaru’s grid has four times as many cells as Recife’s for a quarter of the people: most of the municipality is rural, and its large rural tracts spread a few people over each cell.

Schools and health units

Schools: those of INEP’s catalogue that are public (municipal, state or federal) and open with no restriction, and have coordinates. Health units: the CNES establishments of types 1 (posto de saúde) and 2 (centro de saúde / unidade básica), the primary health care units of the SUS, that are active and have coordinates. Both are taken over the whole area cut from OpenStreetMap, so the nearest unit can be across the municipal border, as it often is for people living near it.

cut_area <- function(k) st_transform(st_read(file.path(data_dir, k, "cut.geojson"),
                                             quiet = TRUE), 4674)

schools_in <- function(area) {
  s <- st_read(schools_file, quiet = TRUE, wkt_filter = st_as_text(st_as_sfc(st_bbox(area))),
               query = paste("SELECT code_school, name_school, name_muni, geom",
                             "FROM schools_2023 WHERE admin_category = 'Pública'",
                             "AND service_restriction = 'ESCOLA EM FUNCIONAMENTO",
                             "E SEM RESTRIÇÃO DE ATENDIMENTO'"))
  s <- s[!st_is_empty(s), ]
  s <- s[lengths(st_intersects(s, area)) > 0, ]
  xy <- st_coordinates(s)
  data.frame(id = as.character(s$code_school), name = s$name_school,
             municipality = s$name_muni, lon = xy[, 1], lat = xy[, 2])
}

cnes <- read.csv2(unz(cnes_file, "cnes_estabelecimentos.csv"), fileEncoding = "latin1",
                  colClasses = "character", na.strings = character())
cnes <- cnes[cnes$CO_UF == "26" & cnes$TP_UNIDADE %in% c("1", "2") &
               cnes$CO_MOTIVO_DESAB == "" & cnes$NU_LATITUDE != "", ]
health_in <- function(area) {
  h <- data.frame(id = cnes$CO_CNES, name = cnes$NO_FANTASIA,
                  municipality_code = cnes$CO_IBGE,
                  lon = as.numeric(cnes$NU_LONGITUDE), lat = as.numeric(cnes$NU_LATITUDE))
  inside <- lengths(st_intersects(st_as_sf(h, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4674), area)) > 0
  h[inside, ]
}

schools <- lapply(setNames(cities$key, cities$key), function(k) schools_in(cut_area(k)))
health <- lapply(setNames(cities$key, cities$key), function(k) health_in(cut_area(k)))
sapply(cities$key, function(k) c(schools = nrow(schools[[k]]), health_units = nrow(health[[k]])))
#>              recife caruaru
#> schools         937     216
#> health_units    511     102

A few things to know about these registers, seen while preparing them:

  • Of the public schools in operation, 22 of 486 in Recife and 15 of 168 in Caruaru have no coordinates in the catalogue and cannot be placed; they are left out.
  • Of the 167 active primary care units registered in Recife, six have coordinates outside the municipality: four a few hundred metres across the border, but one 24 km away, on the Ilha de Itamaracá, and one 20 km away, in Moreno. In Caruaru, two of 75 do, one of them 5 km out. Taking units by where they are rather than where they are registered keeps the far ones out of these figures (they fall outside the cut area), but those units are missing from their own neighbourhoods.
  • Schools and health units sit close to the streets of the extract: the median distance to the nearest street is 7 to 16 m, and a single school in each city is more than 300 m from one (418 m in Recife, 574 m in Caruaru), well within the 1.6 km at which peabiru links a point to the street network.

Travel time to the nearest school and health unit

One travel-time matrix per city, mode and kind of unit, from every cell to every unit; the smallest time of each cell is its time to the nearest one. Driving is free flow (no congestion), and these networks have no elevation. The terrain example recomputes the shares below with slope costs: on foot, within 15 minutes of a health unit, Recife goes from 75.8% to 73.7% and Caruaru from 68.0% to 65.8%, and within 30 minutes or by bicycle very little changes.

nearest <- function(k, mode, limit) {
  out <- st_drop_geometry(grids[[k]])
  for (what in c("schools", "health")) {
    units <- if (what == "schools") schools[[k]] else health[[k]]
    m <- travel_time_matrix(networks[[k]], out, units, mode = mode,
                            max_trip_duration = limit)
    t <- tapply(m$travel_time_p50, m$from_id, min)
    out[[what]] <- unname(t[as.character(out$id)])   # NA: none within the limit
  }
  out
}

share_within <- function(t, minutes) {
  sapply(c("schools", "health"), function(what)
    round(100 * sum(t$population[!is.na(t[[what]]) & t[[what]] <= minutes]) /
            sum(t$population), 1))
}

shares <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cities$key, function(k) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("WALK", "BICYCLE", "CAR"), function(mode) {
    t <- nearest(k, mode, limit = 60)
    data.frame(city = k, mode = mode,
               t(share_within(t, 15)), t(share_within(t, 30)))
  }))
}))
names(shares)[3:6] <- c("school_15", "health_15", "school_30", "health_30")
shares
#>      city    mode school_15 health_15 school_30 health_30
#> 1  recife    WALK      95.6      75.8      99.6      97.5
#> 2  recife BICYCLE      99.5      96.0      99.8      99.8
#> 3  recife     CAR      99.2      99.2      99.2      99.2
#> 4 caruaru    WALK      72.5      68.0      92.7      85.7
#> 5 caruaru BICYCLE      92.7      84.9      97.9      91.1
#> 6 caruaru     CAR      99.8      98.2     100.0      99.9

The table is the share of the population (in %) within 15 and 30 minutes of the nearest public school and primary health care unit. In Recife, 96% of the people live within 15 minutes’ walk of a public school and 76% of a health unit; in Caruaru, 73% and 68%. On a bicycle the gap narrows; by car, with free-flowing traffic, nearly everyone is within 15 minutes of both.

Recife’s driving shares stop at 99.2% for a reason worth knowing: from 17 cells of Boa Viagem (about 12 thousand residents on this grid) there is no car route to the rest of the network on this extract, although the streets connect on foot and by bicycle. Removing every turn restriction from the extract does not reconnect them; the cause is in how the OpenStreetMap data of that area is read for cars, and is not identified yet. Checks like this one (cells or units that a mode never reaches) are worth running on any new extract.

On a map, walking (drawn by site/figures/pernambuco.R in the repository, from these results):

A map like these, with plain ggplot2:

library(ggplot2)
walk <- nearest("recife", "WALK", limit = 60)
cells <- merge(grids$recife[, "id"], walk, by = "id")
p <- ggplot(cells) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(health, c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 60))), colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "OrRd", direction = -1, na.value = "grey85",
                    name = "Minutes") +
  labs(title = "Walking time to the nearest primary health care unit, Recife") +
  theme_void()
ggsave(file.path(tempdir(), "recife-health.png"), p, width = 6, height = 7, dpi = 110)

How many units within reach

The nearest unit is one measure; how many units are within reach is another, which accessibility() computes directly: here, the public schools within 15 minutes’ walk of each cell, and the average over the population.

sapply(setNames(cities$key, cities$key), function(k) {
  a <- accessibility(networks[[k]], st_drop_geometry(grids[[k]]),
                     transform(schools[[k]], n = 1), opportunities_colnames = "n",
                     mode = "WALK", cutoffs = 15)
  people <- grids[[k]]$population[match(a$id, grids[[k]]$id)]
  round(weighted.mean(a$accessibility, people), 1)
})
#>  recife caruaru 
#>     4.6     2.6

On average, a resident of Recife has between four and five public schools within a quarter of an hour on foot; one of Caruaru, between two and three.

Isochrones from the centre

From Marco Zero, in Recife’s old centre, and from the Feira de Caruaru, the area reached in 10, 20 and 30 minutes by each mode, in square kilometres:

centres <- list(
  recife = data.frame(id = "Marco Zero", lon = -34.8709722, lat = -8.063374),
  caruaru = data.frame(id = "Feira de Caruaru", lon = -35.9713866, lat = -8.2897512)
)
iso <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cities$key, function(k) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("WALK", "BICYCLE", "CAR"), function(mode) {
    i <- isochrone(networks[[k]], centres[[k]], mode = mode,
                   cutoffs = c(10, 20, 30), zoom = 11)
    data.frame(city = k, mode = mode, minutes = i$isochrone,
               km2 = round(as.numeric(st_area(st_transform(i, utm))) / 1e6, 1))
  }))
}))
xtabs(km2 ~ mode + minutes + city, data = iso)
#> , , city = caruaru
#> 
#>          minutes
#> mode         10    20    30
#>   BICYCLE   1.3   8.9  23.4
#>   CAR      22.1 285.9 696.4
#>   WALK      0.1   1.5   4.7
#> 
#> , , city = recife
#> 
#>          minutes
#> mode         10    20    30
#>   BICYCLE   0.8   3.0   8.2
#>   CAR       5.7 112.5 367.6
#>   WALK      0.4   1.3   3.0

One number here depends on more than routing: the 20-minute driving polygon of Caruaru has dozens of holes (pockets of the grid not reached in time) that touch each other. isochrone() returns its polygons made valid with sf::st_make_valid() on longitude and latitude (s2), which merges many of those holes into the polygon: 285.9 km². Repaired with GEOS in metres instead, as the Python example does, the same polygon measures 248.9 km². The other polygons agree to 0.1 km².

Variations

  • Another municipality. Change cities: the IBGE code (from https://servicodados.ibge.gov.br/api/v1/localidades/municipios), the buffer, the state of the census tracts (UF/PE/PE_setores_CD2022.gpkg) and of the CNES rows (CO_UF), and the Geofabrik region.
  • Large matrices on disk. With output_dir, travel_time_matrix() and accessibility() write one CSV file per origin instead of returning a data frame: the 4,489 × 216 driving matrix of Caruaru never has to fit in memory.
  • Gradual access. decay_function = "logistic" (or "exponential", "linear") in accessibility() weighs each school by its distance in time instead of counting those under a hard limit.
  • Public transport. With a GTFS feed in the network directory, the same calls take mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"), a departure_datetime and a time_window.
  • A browser map. The isochrone demo has the streets of Recife and of the urban area of Caruaru and draws isochrones wherever you click.
